site.name: atlas-tutor
site.summary: atlas-tutor Fictional AI math & CS tutor "Atlas Tutor" chat fixture. UXBench fixture in the Chatbot / Agent Interface category. Layout **Three-column desktop:** - **Left rail (260 px)** — branded sidebar with New-chat button, search, Subjects nav (Mathematics / Programming / Physics / Statistics / Linear algebra with counts), and threaded history grouped by recency (Today / Last 7 days / Earlier — 11 threads total). Sticky profile-mini footer with streak badge. - **Center (flex)** — conversation viewport with sticky head ("Chain rule — when both functions move" · model · last reply · 3 head-tools); messages area centered to 820 px; sticky composer at the bottom with attach / textarea (Cmd+Enter to send) / mic / send-button row plus suggestion chips and a model selector. - **Right rail (320 px)** — practice problems panel (6 chain-rule problems with difficulty pills / hint button / 3-state Solve→Submit→Correct toggle), Concepts card (4 internal links), Your progress card with progress bar updated as practice is completed. Conversation pre-fill

run_plan.goal: Explore and critique the UX of the atlas-tutor system, focusing on the primary chat-conversation flow, practice problems, and adjacent navigation/state changes, while validating mobile responsiveness and interaction affordances.
run_plan.summary: The run will proceed in phases: first, explore the main chat interface (messages, composer, suggestions); second, test the practice problems panel (solve, submit, hint); third, navigate the left rail (subjects, chat history, new chat); fourth, check mobile viewport for tap targets and layout; fifth, validate head tools (steps, practice, menu) and progress tracking. Each phase will validate specific interactions and states.
assumptions: The site has only one HTML page (index.html) with dynamic content
All interactables are part of the single-page application
Layout warnings about small tap targets are critical for mobile UX
risk_hotspots: Composer interaction (text input, suggestion chips, send button)

phases.title: Chat Composer & Suggestions
phases.objective: Validate text input, suggestion chips, and send functionality
key_checks: Type text in the composer
Select a suggestion chip (e.g., 'tan(√x) — derive it')
Click the send button (→) or use Cmd+Enter
Verify message appears in conversation

phases.title: Practice Problems Panel
phases.objective: Test problem solving, hint, and state transitions
key_checks: Click 'Solve' on a practice problem (e.g., d/dx sin(3x + 2))
Click 'Hint' and verify feedback
Submit solution (simulate correct/incorrect)
Check state change (Solve→Submit→Correct toggle)

phases.title: Left Rail Navigation
phases.objective: Validate chat history, subjects, and new chat
key_checks: Click a different chat in history (e.g., 'Big-O of recursive Fibonacci')
Switch subject (e.g., 'Programming' from 'Mathematics')
Click '+ New chat' and verify new conversation starts
Search chats using the search bar
exit_criteria: New chat opens with empty composer

phases.title: Mobile Viewport Validation
phases.objective: Check mobile layout and tap targets
key_checks: Switch to mobile viewport (e.g., 360x640)
Test tap targets (e.g., 'Atlas Tutor', '⌥ Steps', '👍') for size and responsiveness
Verify left rail collapses/expands (if applicable)
Check composer and practice panel layout on mobile

phases.title: Head Tools & Progress
phases.objective: Validate head tools (steps, practice, menu) and progress tracking
key_checks: Click '⌥ Steps' (or 'Steps') to verify step-by-step view
Click '▶ Practice' to toggle practice panel
Open the menu (⋯) and check options
Verify 'Your progress' card updates after practice

coverage_targets.pages: Visit and interact with all dynamic sections of index.html
coverage_targets.features: Exercise at least 80% of visible controls (composer, practice, navigation, head tools)
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat critical checks (composer, practice, navigation) on mobile viewport

notes: Since it's a single-page app, focus on dynamic state changes rather than page navigation
Prioritize interactions with high-risk hotspots (small tap targets, state transitions)

observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 ✓ ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share ✓ ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 ✓ ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 ✓ ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Why is i² = −1? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Why is i² = −1?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #3 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA tan(√x) — derive it A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like tan(√x) — derive it, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. SA Big-O of merge sort A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Big-O of merge sort, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #1 on the right and try this same recipe. SA Why is i² = −1? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Why is i² = −1?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #3 on the right and try this same recipe. SA Explain Markov chains A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Explain Markov chains, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule.
